description: The social contract is the idea that political authority rests, at least in part, on an understood agreement between a community and those who govern it: people accept laws, obligations, taxation, and military service in exchange for order, protection, justice, and the preservation of the community. Although the term itself belongs mainly to later political philosophy, similar ideas can be seen in ancient societies through Greek citizenship, Roman civic duty, republican institutions, assemblies, law codes, and reciprocal expectations between rulers and subjects. Ancient thinkers such as Plato, Aristotle, and the Sophists debated why people form states and obey laws, while traditions surrounding figures such as Lycurgus or the Roman Republic portrayed political order as dependent upon shared duties between citizens and the state.
